utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the Registry, the counsel for the Prosecution and for the Defence. We will be resuming our work. Before we call in the next witness, I have two small issues to address. First, Mr. Jovan Simic, where do we stand with respect to Mr. Prcac's health? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Mr. Prcac is feeling a bit better. He is not able to attend these hearings. I have been informed that President Jorda will be meeting Mr. McFadden, the commander of the Detention Unit, this morning. I have been asked to be in the Detention Unit at 10.30 to address some transport problems. He feels better, but he's not well enough to attend, and it is my belief that he will be incapacitated until the end of the week. After meeting Mr. Prcac and Mr. McFadden, if he is unable to attend, I have some suggestions for Your Honours. I can go through them now or whenever Your Honours prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, perhaps. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] It is my opinion and my suggestion that if Mr. Prcac is unable to attend the proceedings - and this Defence teams feels that it is absolutely essential that he be present during the cross-examination of Mr. Radic - so as to avoid any loss of time and any upset of the timetable, I would try to abbreviate my case. We could lend a day or two to Mr. Fila, and then I would reduce my time for my case so that we wouldn't upset the timetable while achieving the presence of Mr. Prcac and, at the same time, completing the proceedings as planned. Perhaps you have a better suggestion, and also perhaps the health of Mr. Prcac will improve sufficiently for him to be able to attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your suggestions and information, Mr. Simic. I'll give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers first and then to Mr. Fila to see whether they agree. Ms. Somers, two questions for you: What is the position of the Prosecution regarding the health of Mr. Prcac, and the suggestion that Mr. Jovan Simic has just made regarding the cross-examination of Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first item this morning on my agenda was to speak with Mr. Jovan Simic and ask about the condition of Mr. Prcac. He informed me exactly what he informed the Chamber. Our primary concern, of course, is that he get better and is able to have his own presence at the hearings. In terms of the issue of transport, if that's a question, that is being attended to. That has been discussed, as you did, with President Jorda yesterday. That was also discussed within our own ranks. We are preparing to encapsulate what we said yesterday on the record, a written matter. I have just spoken with Mr. Rohde from the Registry about this. In terms of trying to accommodate the presence or not of Mr. Prcac, I don't know logistically how that would affect their case. As for us, we have, other than the two experts and the one civilian, only Mr. Radic's testimony. It may or may not cause a problem in terms of order. One question I wanted to ask the Chamber is whether or not a monitor is available to Mr. Prcac which may also enable one of the counsel, as they are two counsel, to attend. And then if there were issues to be raised, have a substantial -- have a significant enough break so that whatever Mr. Prcac might say to the second counsel could be relayed to the counsel in court to accommodate potential cross-examination questions. It would just be one possible approach. Otherwise, I would have to leave it in the Chamber's hands as to rearranging the order of testimony, and certainly if, as between counsel, there's an agreement on sharing time, that's something out of our hands. We will try to work with the Chamber and counsel. We certainly understand the problem. Any reasonable suggestion we will certainly try to go on with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Susan Somers. Mr. Fila, your comment regarding Mr. Jovan Simic's suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have spoken to Mr. Simic, Mr. President, and as you noted in connection with Mr. Kvocka's testimony, Mladjo Radic was present and available. And I think that this solution would be a better one, the one suggested by Mr. Simic, to give Mr. Prcac a chance to really recover properly by staying in his cell. But I will accept any ruling of this Trial Chamber, as I am ready to begin with Mladjo Radic after these three witnesses, but I think that Mr. Simic's suggestion continues to be the best one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this matter, the Chamber needs to continue to confer, so we don't have a decision yet, because this is not the moment for a discussion on this matter. We will deal with it later. There is another issue to be addressed before we begin with the testimony, and that has to do with the question of translation that was raised yesterday. I have received a brief memo from the Translation Service, which was also sent to the registry, to Ms. Krystal Thompson, which means that the parties will have copies too, and I wish to tell you what is the upshot of this memo. It is in English, so I'm going to read it in English. [In English] "Reference is made to the B/C/S term 'razvodnik straze,' mentioned at yesterday's hearing at the Kvocka case, page 9212 of the English transcript. We wish to point out that the official CLSS translation of this term has been and remains 'guard shift leader.' This term should not be confused with 'sef smene,'" do you understand, B/C/S, "for which the CLSS translation is 'shift leader.' We are at your disposal for any additional information you may require." [Interpretation] So that is it. The question I have for you now is: Having this information coming from the Translation Unit, and bearing in mind the distinction that we made yesterday between the meaning and the term, a word, and its content, the question is whether we need to do what I suggested yesterday, that is, to hear the original once again, to have it translated - do you have a memo from the Translation Unit? Perhaps we already have it here with us - and then to hear the opinion of the parties. Anyway, I see that Mr. Fila would like to speak, after which I will give Ms. Somers the floor. I think that the position is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your permission, I would like Madam Registrar to give you what I prepared for you, a page from an English/Serbo-Croatian dictionary, with the translation of the term "razvodnik straze," the Benson dictionary. And you will see exactly what it is, and it differs from what the Translation Unit has given you. So there is an adequate term in the English language. It is "corporal of the guard." "Razvodnik straze," according to that dictionary, is "corporal of the guard." So could Madam Registrar please give you a copy of this page. And anyone can perform that function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll be glad to have that from you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have highlighted the term and you will see what it is. Benson is the best-known dictionary, as far as I know, for our language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what is your suggestion, Mr. Fila, in this connection? What do you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we use this term that is provided by Morton Benson, "corporal of the guard," and that is not the term used by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I spoke with the persons, the supervisory personnel at Translation Service, it was explained to me that in fact this dictionary had already been looked at, as had a number of other dictionaries, and I don't think that necessarily the opinion on Benson is shared, but it nonetheless was consulted. And having consulted the dictionaries which are the technical tools of that section of the Tribunal, the persons who have authored that memo have still maintained their position. I think if there is a question about why that was arrived at despite certain non-contextual definitions that are found simply in a dictionary, then perhaps the Chamber could ask for the analysis that goes behind the conclusion. But it was very thoroughly explained to me that all dictionaries relevant had been consulted and that notwithstanding what was in Benson, this particular translation is what is the official one of the unit, and we would, of course, support that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to ask Madam Registrar to give a copy of this memo to the parties. What we believe is that we should admit into evidence these documents, and then it is up to the Chamber to decide. The interpreters already have the terms so I don't think it is necessary to repeat the original version, because everyone knows what the term was that was used. So we are going to admit these documents after they have been given to the parties, and to facilitate things, I can perhaps give my copy to Madam Registrar to copy and give a copy to the parties after the break. I think it is not necessary, after all, to admit into evidence the dictionary because, after all, it is part of the judicial notice. I'm joking. But I don't think it's necessary anyway. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there's one other aspect to this issue that arises out of yesterday's testimony by the witness Delic, because in English, we only heard the term "shift leader" used, and now there appears to be two possibilities, depending on which word in B/C/S is used. The problem is this: When Mr. Fila was questioning Mr. Delic, he apparently used the word "razvodnik straze," which yesterday was translated as "shift leader." When Ms. Somers cross-examined the witness, in English she used the word "shift leader." I don't know what the witness heard in B/C/S, and he answered according to whatever he heard as the B/C/S translation of "shift leader." I think it's important to find out which word the witness heard in B/C/S both when Mr. Fila and Ms. Somers were posing questions, because you'll recall Ms. Somers referred to the Kvocka testimony using the word "shift leader". So there's still a problem in the transcript as it reads from yesterday's questioning of Mr. Fila and the questions of Ms. Somers that were put to Witness Delic, and the only way to resolve it is to hear what the witness Delic heard when Ms. Somers used the word "shift leader." Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. O'Sullivan, do you have a suggestion, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the easiest solution is to request CLSS to listen to the audiotapes and then they can prepare a memo as they've done on this other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an idea too. I haven't consulted my colleagues. We could call the witness to the witness box once again to clear up the matter, Mr. O'Sullivan. What do you think? If the witness is still available. I think he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's one solution. But I think the record would be clearer based on what was said in court yesterday, because what Mr. Fila said in B/C/S was rendered into English and what Ms. Somers said in English was rendered into B/C/S, and based on this determination we have this morning, we can see which is the correct terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. O'Sullivan, if I understand your point - and I think it is a good one - due to the fact that we have a concept used by Mr. Fila translated in one way and then Ms. Somers used that translation, the witness was able to respond in a different manner. So if the witness had a good translation, the answer could have been different. Do you understand my point?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make a correction in the transcript, in my opinion, would not resolve the problem because, after all, it is an interpretation. The question is to see whether the question was put to the witness using the proper term, and what his response would be. Would it be the same or not? That is my question, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Given that the witness is still here, on those limited matters, perhaps he can be questioned. But there is certainly confusion in the transcript right now based on what we've determined this morning regarding terminology, or there may be. I don't know what he heard in B/C/S when Ms. Somers questioned him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Fila waving to indicate the witness has already left. Did I understand you correctly, your signs?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is probably at the airport, I don't know that, but he left this morning at 7.30. If I may make a very simple suggestion which I think would resolve the problem. You have received a memo from the Translation Service as to what I said, the word I used, "razvodnik straze," and how the witness responded. We also know what Ms. Somers said in English. She said "shift leader." So there is no dispute over that. The only thing that is disputed is what the witness heard as an interpretation of what Ms. Somers said, so how the term "shift leader" was interpreted to the witness. There are two possibilities: Either it was translated as "razvodnik straze," which is wrong, or as "sef smene," which is correct and which I did hear. If the Translation Unit were to check Ms. Somers' translation, they will be able to write a memo to tell you that the term used by Ms. Somers, "shift leader," was translated as "sef smene." Then it will be easy for you to decide regarding both points. That would be my suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, after which I'll give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers. Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully appreciate everything that has been said. It is one aspect of the problem which I have every understanding for. However, this translation that has been offered to us by the Translation Service absolutely does not correspond to what a razvodnik straze does. It causes a whole lot of confusion. The word here used is "guard shift leader," a leader of a guard shift. That does not exist. The memo we distributed this morning corresponds to what a razvodnik straze actually does in the military. Razvodnik straze is an ordinary soldier, a private, whose only task is to distribute the guards. He is not a leader; he does not have the status of leader. This can mislead the Trial Chamber, this term, because it uses the word "leader of the guard shift." The duties of an ordinary policeman in a shift were similar to those of a razvodnik straze, a guard distributor, literally. This is not just a matter of linguistics. It is a far more serious issue which can cause very serious consequences, which can have very serious consequences, and that is why I believe that this question needs to be clarified, or at least for the Translation Service to give us the explanation of the functions and activities of a person they describe as guard shift leader, because that, in my opinion, is the gist of the matter, in addition to the simply linguistic aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic, we are not going to go on with this discussion. I think it is difficult for us to ask of the Translation Service to describe the tasks of that guard. I think for the Translation Service, all we can expect them to do is give a translation. The content is something that belongs more properly within your responsibilities. But, in any event, we are not going to continue this discussion. I will give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers and, after that, we will review the matter. Since we have already eliminated the possibility of calling back the witness, as he has left, we will reconsider the matter and take a decision. But, in any event, we will not do that without consulting you. Ms. Susan Somers, to wind up this discussion on translation, otherwise we will go on forever, do you have any comment to make in response to what Mr. Fila has just suggested and the remarks made by Mr. Krstan Simic? Quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I was just checking yesterday's transcript to indicate that I had read a direct quote from the transcript of the Kvocka cross-examination. I think it would probably be a good idea to have the Translation Service listen to the tapes to hear what was asked of Mr. Delic on both occasions, and that perhaps would put the matter in better light, and then leave it, perhaps, as an issue ultimately for argument. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will take into consideration your suggestions, for which I thank you. Perhaps I will consult the Translation Service to get this memo from them. Anyway, we will decide later. I think it is time to go on and call the next witness who is waiting. Mr. Fila, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all three witnesses are here, and that is good news. In consultation with Ms. Somers, I shall start off with the witness left over from yesterday, and then we're going to have two expert witnesses. The Defence now calls witness Branko Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Branko Starcevic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Draw closer to the microphone, please, and try to stand as comfortably as possible. Make yourself comfortable. Thank you for coming. You will start off by answering questions put to you by Mr. Fila. Mr. Fila, your witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Omarska on the 2nd of December, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What schooling have you had?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Eight years of primary school and a driver's test.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did you work at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning I worked in the Cajavec, Rudi Cajavec firm, and later on I worked in Austria for nine years. From Austria, I returned and now work in the Prijedor Bank as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Since when have you been working in the Prijedor Bank?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Since 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you married? Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married and have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were you in the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In the army, I was a Corporal, a Private First Class.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Private First Class, which in B/C/S was said "razvodnik." So the interpreter notes, whether it's Private First Class or Corporal, in B/C/S it was Razvodnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, once again we have "razvodnik straze."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In April 1992, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I was called up and I reported to Omarska and I was distributed to do village guards or village watch at the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that in Omarska proper, in the village of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long did you spend in Omarska proper, the town?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I spent about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened next, after that month?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, there were no more village watches. We had to go to the battlefront. And as I was older, they assigned me to the mine, to provide security for the hangars in the mine, to safeguard the hangars in the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you accepted being -- to do this assignment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was an older man and it was easier for me to provide security for the hangar rather than go to the battlefront.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know that there were people there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know there were people there. I thought I'd just be guarding the machines inside, the mine machines and machinery used in the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened next? How did you get to Omarska and when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a commander came to fetch me. We were boarded into a vehicle and taken to the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many of you were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: There were about 15 to 20 of us. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And were you all reservists?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were all reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Of the army. The Territorial Defence, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you arrived there, what did you see and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I was astounded when I saw the number of people who were there. I did not know what to do. I met comrade Kvocka and said, "What are we going to do? And he said, "Well, I don't know. I don't know what you're going to do." And then I came across a guard. He took us in and said, "You're going to go with us and we're going to distribute you because you're in our shift."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What happened to the officer who took you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He suddenly disappeared. He just left us there, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what happened next with you? What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Another reservist came up to us and said that we were going to replace them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he military or police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a military man from the TO, the Territorial Defence, the army, and he led us off. And we replaced each one of the others, and so we would replace them regularly and be replaced regularly, relieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long were you relieved in this way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there for one day, for example, and then the other one would come for the night, and that was how we relieved ourselves, in this regular fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this 12/24, 12/24 rhythm [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many months were you there for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I was there until August. I was there until August. I came with a bicycle for the last time. I didn't find anyone there. I just found a guard who said, "The people have gone and there's nothing more for you to do here."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I returned home and reported to the Prijedor Bank and continued driving, as I had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To put something right that appeared in the transcript, did you say that the shifts were 12/12/24?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where was your guard post within the compound?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: My guard post was in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What side? The side facing the "white house" or the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was opposite the petrol pump.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Inside the hangar or outside?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many people were there in the hangar with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Throughout the time you spent at this guard post and up to the time that you left Omarska, did you ever report to somebody about what happened during your shift?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No. We had nobody to hand over a report to because there were no officers or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you under the command of the police or army, or under no command at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Under no command at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you arrived, did you see uniforms in that part of the Omarska centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I saw military uniforms, the SMB olive-green/grey uniforms that we wore, and the policemen, who wore blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any special-unit people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the first days they provided security, and these special units left after a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: They were a special unit. They were masked. You couldn't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were they from Omarska or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not from Omarska. They were some kind of special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that of the active policemen, you once saw Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see him later on as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see any other active policemen whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Radic as well, and once I --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know Mladjo Radic before the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was he before the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you socialise with him? Did you meet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did meet. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us make a distinction. Were you intimate friends with him or just an acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was just an acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you were born in Omarska, were you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Srednja Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know him from then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see any detainees in the Omarska centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In the centre of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where you stood guard in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what they looked like, what happened to them, why they were there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Why they were there I have no idea, but they were tired, they had suffered, they were dirty. And what else can I tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a smell of any kind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a stench, a bad smell, and every day I had to wash myself and wash my clothes to wash the smell out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any running water; and if so, where, and did you drink it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were taps, and we drank that water and they drank that water, and there was no other water but the water that came through the taps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any toilets where the people could relieve themselves?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you happen to notice or hear during your stay there that the people were beaten?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when those special unit people were there, then there was beating. But later on, everything calmed down, when we took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see or hear that there were any dead?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did hear that there were dead when those special unit people were there, but not later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you happen to see any?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not because I was in another place altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should now like to draw your attention to the contact with Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was he there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At one point you met him.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, once in his office, and we had a cup of coffee. He asked me to take to his kum some food, to the hangar, and that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the kum's name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was Fazlic. Midhat Fazlic, I think. Because he was a kidney patient, his kidneys were poor, and Radic said to me, "He has this kidney condition. Please help," and I helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he help any other people that you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Whenever there was some bread left over or anything else, any other food left over, I would take it to the people and they would distribute it, because they were hungry and were not very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why didn't he take this himself but asked you to do it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was not permitted to go down there. He was upstairs, doing his duty; he was by the telephone, that kind of thing. He was sorry because there were a lot of people he knew there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was he afraid of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was he afraid of? Why didn't he dare go himself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were lots of people he knew there, lots of people from Ljubija. They knew him and he said, "I can't go because I feel sorry for those people. I can't go, so you please take these things instead of me."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he afraid to go?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he was permitted to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why would he be afraid?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he felt uncomfortable, because when you see the people from Ljubija, the people he lived and worked with, he was sorry and didn't like to go. He felt uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you saw him in an office, drinking coffee.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whose office was that? What was the office used for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a sort of waiting room with a telephone, his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who used that office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Everybody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did it say anything on the door of this office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it upstairs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was on an upper story.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there many people there when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were always lots of people passing by, going to and fro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any civilians there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any investigators from the MUP or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should like to clarify one point. In your opinion, could Mladjo Radic order you to do anything?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he could not order us anything. He didn't order us anything, nor did he contact us at all. He didn't have any contact with us either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would any of the other counsel like to ask any questions? Mr. Simic is on his feet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that when you were brought to Omarska you met Kvocka by chance.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the individual whom you said you thought to be Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean "the name"?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was Kvocka's name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Kvocka, Kvocka -- I've forgotten. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you know that Kvocka, that man Kvocka, from before?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Where did you know him from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: From Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did he work for a long time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: After that first meeting, you never saw him again, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any other Defence counsel? I see negative signs coming from the Defence counsel. Now we have the Prosecution, and it is Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Starcevic, you will now be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution. Mr. Waidyaratne, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, when you were called up to the TO, you were a driver attached to the Prijedor Bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you were called up in April, were you given a uniform?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you provided with a weapon, a gun?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, some old rifles, M-48s.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you worked in the checkpoint. Where exactly was your checkpoint during the month of April?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Those were village guards. We only guarded villages and we checked vehicles travelling so as to prevent anybody from entering the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, my question, please try to understand. I'm sure it is a very clear question. Where was this checkpoint? Can you give us the location?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In the village. In the village, in Srednja Omarska village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, thereafter, you said that you agreed to go to the Omarska mine without going to the battlefield. What was the date that you went to Omarska for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was late May. I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were the others who went with you to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Why, there were some 15 or 20 of us. I cannot recall their names now. All I know is that there were about 15 or maybe 20 of us. We were all elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you say that you're an elderly person. But, say, ten years ago, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was about 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you can't remember any of those people who went with you, who worked with you for more than one month and thereafter who went to Omarska with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I remember a few of them. I remember a few of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please give us their names.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Uros Vuceta.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is it Uros?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Uros, U-r-o-s. Rajko Vuceta.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Rajko Vuceta?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Can you remember any other names?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Nedjo Vuceta.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Nedjo Vuceta?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, these people also went to the Omarska camp with you; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And they were in the same shift that you worked in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not on my shift. They were relieving us or, rather, I relieved them and they relieved me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see Radic in Omarska often?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not that often because he was in a different building from the one that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you remember that you gave a statement to the Defence counsel, Mr. Ranko Darkic, an attorney? Do you remember giving a statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did give it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In that statement you said the truth, according to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, when you were in Omarska, what was the shift that you worked in? In whose shift did you work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Radic's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic's shift. Do you remember any other persons in Mr. Radic's shift?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I used to see comrade Kos too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What is this comrade Kos' first name? Is it Milojica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, he was also from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He was a reservist.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, where did he stand guard when he was on duty?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I could not know that because I did not see them. I saw him once or twice perhaps, not more than that, and I do not know where he stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, when you went into the Omarska camp, you said that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you met comrade Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who is this Kvocka? How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I knew him from civilian times and I knew him as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And he was an active-duty policeman; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you gave a statement, which I mentioned earlier. Did you say it was Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Miroslav, Miroslav. It had slipped my memory. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you knew him before the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, when you met Miroslav Kvocka, what exactly did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He told me, "You look after yourselves. You must fend for yourselves. I have nothing to do with you."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did he ask you to organise yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did he say that, if necessary, to speak to any other guard who had been there before you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Another guard came who had already been there, and took us there and told us that we would take over shifts from them and they would take shifts from us, so that we should come to stand guard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I'm asking as to what Mr. Kvocka said. Did he ask you to speak to any other guards who had been there before you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He said, "You manage for yourselves," and at that moment a guard came and said, "You are relieving us."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When Mr. Kvocka said, "You manage yourselves," what exactly did you understand by that? Did you go to -- after that discussion, did you go to a place? Did you go to the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: We went to the hangar, and a Territorial member met us there, said, "You come with us," and the policeman had nothing to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that you were on the side of the petrol pump.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it on the side of the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was opposite the "white house". From the petrol pump, from pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to show the witness a photograph of the Omarska camp to exactly point out as to where he says this petrol pump is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have your permission? This exhibit, which has been marked and admitted, 3/93, I would seek your permission to show this to the witness and to be placed on the ELMO. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, please have a look at the photograph which is there. That is a photograph which is taken from a model of the Omarska camp. And could you point out as to where -- could you see those buildings in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, can you point out the place -- the "white house" which is there, which is in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In the photograph.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, where was the petrol pump?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Here, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: On the other side. On the other side of the hangar building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Not on the side of the "white house", but on the other side of the big building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: On the other side, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were inside the hangar building when you did your guard duty?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you there -- you served in the Omarska camp for almost two months or three months. Were you there during this entire period, inside the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And what time did you come to work, and to whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would arrive around 6.00 or 7.00, take over from my friend. He would go home. And that is how we alternated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And what time did you normally leave the workplace, the mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: As soon as my relief arrives, I go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And what were you asked to do there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: We were asked to guard, to see that nobody gets in and that nobody gets out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, guard in the sense -- whom were you guarding? Was it the detainees?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Both the detainees and the machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And who told you this, as to what you should do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: From those who were before me, who had already been assigned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it the guards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you know about any other shift leaders who were there? Did you know any shift leaders?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness never once said the words "shift leader." Not only that he did not know any shift leaders, he never used the word. During his examination-in-chief, not once were the words "shift leader" used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's why I -- when I realised that he didn't do, I used --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time is already up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was anybody in charge of the shifts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You spoke about Mr. Radic calling you to the office in the administration building.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't call me. I was just passing by and he invited me to drop by and have a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How many times did you go to the office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not go to the office. I did have a cup of coffee there once, but I didn't really go there to see him often.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, you said that you passed by the administration building; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I went to have my lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you have your lunch?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: We had our lunch in the administration building. Below the administration building there was a restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you used to go there almost daily to have your lunch?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this office that you spoke of, in which floor was this office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Second floor, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That was above the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you went and -- when you met Mr. Radic, who else? Were you alone with Mr. Radic or were there any other people in that office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: At that occasion I was alone with Radic because he had invited me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when he was alone, he made this suggestion to you to take the food to Mr. Fazlic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It is. He asked me. He said, "Will you please take this food to him, because he has a kidney complaint. So come, please; help him. Take this food to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did he have the food with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It was on some other occasion that he wanted you to take the food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When did he ask you to take the food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, will you please take care of the time you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have one more minute. I would appreciate it if I am given that opportunity, Your Honour. I would beg you to have that one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think it is one minute, but, yes, I give you that one minute. Yes, please, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you know that Mr. Fazlic was in the hangar building at the time that Mr. Radic asked you for that request?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Fazlic was where I was; in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know at the time that Fazlic was in the hangar building when Mr. Radic asked you to help him, or did Mr. Radic tell you that Mr. Fazlic was in the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, because I knew Fazlic. I knew Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you knew Fazlic was detained in the hangar building; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Fazlic and Fazlic complained to me, telling me that he had this kidney problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radic ask you to look after Mr. Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne, I do not know if the Prosecution has a watch. But if you do have a watch, I believe that your minute lasts longer than 60 seconds; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: There are no more questions, Your Honour. I conclude. The witness had not answered that last question. Thank you. After he finishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, could you kindly answer that last question, please. Did Mr. Radic ask you to look after Mr. Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, he did, because he was a very ill man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Fila, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only to clarify a couple of points.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many times did you see Radic during your stay in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In Omarska, you mean, or in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the camp.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him a few times. I cannot really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you say "a few times," two or three times? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you conclude on those two or three occasions if he had any position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You say that you were on Radic's shift. Does that mean that you were on the same shift with him on those two or three occasions? Does it mean that you were there at the same time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was on my shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you use the word "reservist," a reservist said to you this and that, do you mean a reserve Territorial member, as you were yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So a reservist, a Territorial member, told you to go and guard whatever, wherever you then went to guard.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did those reservists and policemen have anything in common?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This petrol pump that was shown you, now, how far is it; 100 metres, 200 metres?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: About 200, 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, do you have any additional questions? No? Very well. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Before you went to Omarska, how far did this acquaintance with Mr. Radic exist? Were you simply acquaintances or friends?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: We were acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were acquaintances. Now, when you were in the camp, you would pass by his office and he would invite you to have coffee. This office was the office of the administrator? What was this office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Just an ordinary room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There were many offices like that? Everybody had their office? Every guard had an office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You wouldn't know that. You said that there were also investigators coming into the office. Was this office used for investigation too, or were they coming to give reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No. I do not know where the investigators were. I do not know where they conducted their investigations, because I had coffee with Radic only once and I do not know anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What did you see them doing in this office? You said they would be coming in. For coffee?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Where? I don't understand the question. Which office?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The office of Mr. Radic where you went for coffee. You said that the investigators would be coming in. What would they be doing in this office?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my apologies, but Judge Riad is mentioning investigators and the witness said that he was alone with Radic and had coffee with him. He never said it was Radic's office; he never said that the investigators went into that office. I do not know what to say. My apologies, but I do not think we should put into the witness' mouth something that he had not said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [as interpreted] Mr. Fila, the witness repeated several times, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I heard he said lots of people would pass by the office and investigators would go in, and the transcript is there. If the witness says that, then I have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The only time I saw the investigators would be when they arrived in a bus. But I never saw where they went, what room they entered. And I do not know the offices. The only office I had been into was Radic's, and after that, I never went there again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The investigators did not come into this office. You said before that they came into this office, and I noted it down. Did you see them in the office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I did not. I did not see them do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Radic had to stay upstairs and he would not take the food to his friend Fazlic because he stayed upstairs, doing his duty. What did you mean by "doing his duty"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean being on duty upstairs, like me being on duty in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: His duty was upstairs, you mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What would be his duty, in your opinion; to sit in the office or to walk around? What was his duty?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know what his duties were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said his duty kept him upstairs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I do not know that. Did he have to or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke that you worked in Mr. Radic's shift.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What would be his role in this shift? Why do you call it Radic's shift?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just like that, I cannot really say. It could be anyone. I said that I was on Radic's shift because we went together, as if we would be going to work. But he went in that direction and I went to the hangars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, was he commanding the shift? Was he directing the shift?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were just simply acquaintances before, but he asked you to take the food -- to take the medicine to Mr. Fazlic. Would he ask any guard to do such things?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he'd ask any guard to do that. Or did he ask me simply because I was in the hangar? Because I was there and also Midhat was in the same place, Midhat was there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he know that you were a friend of Midhat Fazlic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But were you acquainted with Fazlic? Were you a friend of his?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had met in the camp; we came to know each other down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. I should like to avail myself of this opportunity to make a correction in the transcript. No, it's not really a correction. On page 35:18, at the end of Mr. Fila's intervention, what I said was that the witness will answer, and the transcript in English says: [In English] "Mr. Fila, the witness repeated several times, that is correct." [Interpretation] I did not say that. What I said, and I repeat it to make it quite clear, I said, "Mr. Fila, the witness will answer," and that is it. We already discussed this. We have here this record. All right. I now give the floor to Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness, you said that during the month of April, you were working or guarding at a checkpoint in Omarska centre, or in Omarska. Now, during that period, did you have anybody in command over you? Did you have anybody that told you what to do or gave you orders? This is at the checkpoint now, not at the camp. Did you have a chain of command that you were in at the checkpoint - not the camp; at the checkpoint in Omarska - somebody that told you what to do, gave you orders, you reported to, at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us, I believe, that when you came to the camp -- and I'm reading from your statement, but I believe your testimony was, in conformity: "We didn't have a commander or anyone over us, and all we had to do was keep to agreements, come regularly and punctually, and be responsible for our own organisations." In essence, I believe you said this morning that one of the Territorial reservists who was already on duty told you what the shift was, what the hours were, and you agreed to take over his post at the hangar. Is that basically right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did that particular Territorial reservist, or the person you made this agreement to take over this post, did he stay in the camp after you came and took over his post or did he leave?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: He left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: He left. So if nobody -- okay. If nobody was over you or you didn't have a commander, as you said, that all you had to do was keep to the agreement and come regularly and punctually, what would happen if you didn't? If the Territorial reservist was no longer there and there wasn't anybody over you, could you, in effect, change your post, go somewhere else, not come punctually, not come regularly? Did that happen? If the people that made these agreements on the first day left and your people replaced them, nobody was there to enforce the agreement; is that right? So did everybody just come every day, even though there was nobody to make them do it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: One had to attend. One had to come and take over from somebody else. So you had to come. You had to be present. You couldn't allow anyone to stay on guard for 24 hours. I mean, everybody has to go home once in a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you say you had to, what does that mean? I mean, you had to. Was that just something you felt within yourself or that something would happen to you, somebody would do something if you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the wartime labour obligation and also human obligation, to relieve another man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So that if some days somebody didn't show up on their guard post -- I mean, maybe they were sick or maybe something happened and somebody didn't show up on their guard post, what would happen? Who would take over somebody's guard post that just didn't come?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he would have to find a friend and ask him to go in his stead, or somebody else from the same shift, or anyone, or from a different shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So it was up to the -- you're telling us it was up to that guard to make his own arrangements for a substitute; nobody else would order anybody to do it in his place. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. When you came on your shift, did you check in with anybody, like a duty officer or anybody, say, "I'm here," or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No. There was no duty officer that you checked in to to say that you were there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was there anybody -- if you were inside the hangar shift, the prisoners couldn't stay there all the time. I mean, they went out to lunch and they had to go to the bathroom, I assume, at certain times. There were certain reasons why they could go outside the hangar. How would you know that, or how would you know it was all right to let the prisoners go out a certain time? Did anybody else come and say, "We want these prisoners to come with us now," other guards, other soldiers would say to you? Well, how did you know when it was time for them to go to lunch, or what if they had to go to the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, they would let us know when the lunch is and then people would all go to lunch. If the weather was nice, they could go out into the yard and have a walk and get some fresh air, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Nobody came and said at lunchtime, "Your people can come to lunch now. A group of your people can come to lunch"? They just went when they felt like it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No. From the restaurant, somebody would come. When the lunch would be ready, they would come and tell us, "Yes, people can come to have lunch."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would that be a guard, or who from the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Cooks, as a rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So people who were just civilian workers in the restaurant would come and say -- would go all around the camp and say, "Okay, it's lunchtime, your people can come now"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. If something happened while you were on shift, I mean, if a disturbance of any kind came, what would you do? Who would you go to? If a prisoner tried to escape, just say, or two prisoners got in a fight or something unusual happened on the shift and you weren't able to take care of it yourself, where would you go? What would you do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I would have to inform the guards, but there were no such occasions in my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Who? But you must have had in your mind, as a good reservist, what you would do if one arose. Who would you go to to get help?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: There were no problems, and I don't really know who I would go to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you weren't prepared, in your own mind -- if some kind of disturbance or emergency happened, you didn't know what you would do, how you would get help?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what I would do, nor did I get any such orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. And nobody ever -- not orders, but nobody ever told what you should do if something happened? If, for instance, you were told -- you did tell us that somebody at some point said your job was to prevent other people from coming in or these prisoners from getting out; is that right? I mean, that was your idea of what your job was, to make sure nobody got -- that shouldn't came in or the prisoners didn't get out? Is that fair to say what you thought your guarding job was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the job of a guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Now, if a person tried to escape -- I know they didn't on your shift, but if a person tried to escape, you, as a policeman, would have been caught between running after the person to try to prevent them and still guarding all the rest of the people in the hangar. You must have -- well, let me just say: Did you have any plans?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I am not a policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, you were -- okay. You were a reservist guard or -- what would you say you were? How would you describe what you were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I was a guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. But as -- all right. As a guard, you didn't have -- you had not formulated in your own mind any -- what you would do in the circumstance where you were caught between trying to run after a prisoner and remained to guard the remaining prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: What I would do? I would probably let that one man go and guard the others. I wouldn't run after him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question: You said, I believe, that at one point you thought - you thought - Mr. Radic wanted you to take food to his friend in the hangar because he wasn't permitted to go down where the detainees were. If nobody -- if there was no commander in the station and Mr. Radic was just, in your view, an ordinary policeman, but there was nobody over anybody, who would have told him? Who did you think could have told him that he couldn't go down among the detainees? Where would he have gotten any such prohibition from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Starcevic, we have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you a safe journey home. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I see Mr. Fila on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence calls Stanko Bejatovic, our expert witness, an expert on the Criminal Code, and he will be cross-examined by the Prosecution using 20 minutes of their time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Usher, please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question of the comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not clear of the distinction, "20 minutes of their time." This is part of the Defence case and we simply are asking for a bit of cross. I'm not quite clear what the distinction in time was there. Perhaps I could ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this was an idea suggested to us by Mr. Fila, that is, that he is offering the report as the examination-in-chief and then you will cross-examine for 20 minutes, and after that Mr. Fila will have the chance to ask additional questions. Why? I think you understand it very well, why this has been decided. You objected to the admission of the report without cross-examination, so the Chamber felt that you should have an occasion to cross-examine on the points which prompted your objection. You have 20 minutes for clarification, but you will begin immediately, as you have the report already. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think perhaps I wasn't clear. I understand that we have 20 minutes, and we're very grateful to the Chamber for giving us the opportunity. It was "of our time" -- it's not being ticked off from time that we have available for our own case. In other words, this is, as part of the Defence's case, a standard cross-examination - that's all I'm trying to clarify - and it's limited to 20 minutes. That's my understanding; is that correct? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as you know, I have two more days left, Thursday, Friday, and you owe me one day. So all I have is three and a half days which I will not use up. But all I wanted to say was that the Prosecution has 20 minutes so that it shouldn't be 40 minutes. But I didn't want to be too explicit about it. That was my meaning.
