utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us have the witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bejatovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bejatovic, you are here to answer questions which will be put to you by the Prosecutor. So, in a sense, your report represents the examination-in-chief, and we have given the opportunity to Madam Prosecutor 20 minutes to ask you questions to clarify certain points. So, Ms. Susan Somers, you have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Professor Bejatovic, the cases before this Tribunal for which you have prepared expert reports, would you be kind enough to tell us, please, which they are?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, I should like to make a brief remark. In the report that I filed, I saw that there was an error under paragraph 8, second sentence. It has been misinterpreted that a prison punishment for rape is "around the maximum." It should say "around the minimum."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We apologise. We do not have a copy.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: In preparing my report, I relied on the legal practice of present-day Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, and the former Yugoslavia linked to the criminal offence of rape. So I have reviewed the cases of rape in former Yugoslavia and present-day Yugoslavia, and on the basis of that analysis, I have compiled my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Could you tell us, please, which cases before the entire Yugoslavian Tribunal you have provided reports for?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: I only had one report in the Foca case, which was terminated, I think, a month ago. That is the only case in which I participated before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a testifying witness, yes. As a consultant, no other cases at all either, as a non-testifying consultant? That's it, just one?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No, I have not been a consultant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I just want to make sure, for the order of things, the expert statement that you provided in the Kunarac case, which is referred to as the Foca case, was dated 3 July 2000, filed 4 July, and that was the sole report, as I understand it from your testimony, that you filed, other than in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you also gave live testimony in the Kunarac case. I believe it was 11 September 2000. Do you recall coming to the Chamber on behalf of -- I believe one of the Defence counsel had asked you to come in, and you gave live testimony in front of Judges Mumba, Hunt, and Pocar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked -- principally, the concern of the Prosecution in that case was the aggravating factors which were considered in practice before the courts of the former Yugoslavia. And I would like to ask if -- when you were in the cross-examination phase of your testimony, do you recall being asked about certain factors that were not spelled out in your particular report? And I would specifically ask if you recall a question to you by the Prosecutor about ethnically-based motives as an aggravating factor in rape in the former Yugoslavia in sentencing. The question was: "However, an ethnically-based motive would be considered an aggravating factor, wouldn't it, when it comes to sentencing?" Your answer was: [As read] "Certainly. If these motives were to be established, that is, for these motives the crime was committed, if this were to be proven, that is, that those motives -- that these were the motives with which this was committed." So ethnically-based motives behind the act of rape would in fact be considered an aggravating factor under the practice in the former Yugoslavia; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: I said that, but the following should be borne in mind: In the judicial practice of former Yugoslavia and present-day Yugoslavia linked to rape, such motives were never established in a single case; only if, through evidence, it were to be established that such motives existed would that apply, but such motives were never established in the former Yugoslavia or in the present-day Yugoslavia. And this is something that I wish to underline. There were no such motives ever established in any case of rape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: However, should they have been, or if they are in another case -- well, should they have been established, then ethnically-based motives would have been, as I understand your testimony, an aggravating factor. That would just be a yes or a no, if you can help us, please.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I need to add that, according to Yugoslav Criminal Code and judicial practice, no individual factor can be judged in isolation. They are always judged in combination with all the other factors and circumstances. But if there was evidence to confirm that particular element alone, then only then would that apply. But according to Yugoslav criminal law, all the circumstances are judged together and in combination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I think that's understood from your paper. But it was -- what I'm trying to understand from you is that the answer is: Yes, if everything else was looked at as it should be, then ethnically-based motives would be among the mix of aggravating factors to be considered. That's essentially what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: On condition that that is proven, that such motives existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Of course. Another question that was asked of you, and I wanted to make sure it was perfectly clear, was: Would it be an aggravating circumstance if the crime of rape were committed against a very weak or vulnerable person, physically weakened, or a detainee, for example? And your answer was -- Sorry. In fairness, let me give you the entire scenario. You were asked: "Beside the mitigating and aggravating factors you have already listed and told us, would it be an aggravating factor if the crime was committed against a particularly vulnerable person, for instance, detained persons?" Your answer: "If that were to be established, that would certainly be an aggravating circumstance." Then the question was again put to you: "And would it be an aggravating circumstance if the person - I'm sorry - if the crime was committed against a very weak person, physically weak person?" And your answer: "Well, you see, that is estimated in each and every particular case. If it were to be proven that the person concerned, because of his physical capacities, was not in a position to offer any resistance and did not offer any resistance --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "... then that is to be taken into account. However, in view of his or her physical constitution, if he or she was in a position to offer resistance, then that would also be taken into account." And then you go on below to say: "If a victim, for physical reasons, could not offer resistance for various reasons, then that is different."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For counsel and the Chamber, that is on the transcript from Kunarac at page 5391 and the page before it, 5390.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall that particular interaction between you and the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And so for purposes of our understanding, the fact that an alleged victim might be either vulnerable because of detention or physical condition would also be an aggravating factor to be taken into account with the mix of aggravating factors. Would that be a fair statement, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you keep underlining one fact which cannot be accepted. You keep insisting on one factor in isolation from others. A person may be physically very weak and that may not be considered an aggravating circumstance because that fact must be considered in combination with all the other factors. What I'm trying to say, that in the judicial practice of former Yugoslavia and present-day Yugoslavia, we did have cases when the victims of such a crime were physically extremely weak, but that fact was not considered an aggravating circumstance. Why? Because even such victims, in quite a number of cases, by their conduct and certain other circumstances, contributed to the commission of that crime, so that generally speaking, that fact in itself cannot be considered an aggravating factor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your comment about the detained person, the status of being a detained person, if it were considered with all other factors, which I think you've indicated is a must in an analysis of mitigating factors, then that also would be an aggravating factor if properly viewed in context; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: It may, but need not. It need not necessarily be an aggravating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It could be considered -- it could be assessed to see whether it is an aggravating circumstance. Perhaps I should be a bit more clear. It may or may not, but it could be assessed and considered a possible aggravating circumstance, depending?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: You see, according to our legislation - and not only the Yugoslav Criminal Code, but according to most Criminal Codes - no individual circumstance when sentencing can a priori, in itself, be considered an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. aggravating or a mitigating circumstance. In one case it may be one, and in another, another. So we cannot give a clear answer as to what would be the case in a particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. Doctor, Professor, I'm not asking you to say that any one; I'm saying that among the factors could be considered would be detention status, among the factors, as a possible aggravating factor. Yes or no? I mean, this was your testimony. Do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: That factor has to be taken into consideration but in the context that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask about -- I'm sorry. Did you want to say something else, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: In that connection, I wanted to underline another fact. As an individual who is also president of the association for criminal law, I have monitored certain such cases that occurred in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and let me tell you one of the conclusions I reached. I was told on one occasion that in a collection centre where there were quite a large number of detained, relatively young male and female persons, and where they were detained for up to a month, I was told by the detainees that there were cases when those persons themselves initiated certain sexual relationships with the guards who were in those collection centres. So you see, that also is a factor that has to be taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Professor Bejatovic, when you were asked to prepare this paper by counsel for Mr. Radic - I want to clarify something - were you asked to do a study in connection with rape in peacetime or rape in a wartime, armed conflict setting? Do your comments, your observations, in your paper reflect a peacetime setting or a wartime setting for this particular case?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: My report applies to the regulations on this criminal act and the judicial practice of the former Yugoslavia and the present-day Yugoslavia, and that was clearly stated in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The reason I ask is that in the Kunarac case you were asked about whether or not you had considered rape in connection with, I believe, the genocide statutes, which are wartime related, and you indicated that you were told -- the question was:

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In this particular case we are dealing with here in this courtroom, we are talking about war crimes. You are aware of this, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was told that it is the crime of rape that is being considered here. That is what I was told. Not war crimes. I have been informed that this is a classical crime of rape, that that is what the indictment says. And the crime of rape is something quite different from Article 142 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia. Now, that confusion that may or may not have persisted during the Kunarac case, was it clarified to you by Mr. Fila, or whichever counsel you dealt with, that your report would deal with situations involving armed conflict, wartime?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any such discussions. But I would like to say the following in that connection: According to our criminal legislation, and as far as I know, all comparative Criminal Codes do not provide for rape as a war crime. In view of that, I don't think such an act, such a crime, can be considered a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Have you been involved with any cases yourself in the former Yugoslavia where persons were prosecuted for rape of detainees or prisoners during time of conflict?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Not actively. But through the media, through various scientific meetings, we did discuss instances of rape that occurred during the conflicts in the territories of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the testimony in Kunarac, then, you did become aware through cross-examination that the thrust of the issues before this Tribunal deal with rape in an armed conflict setting; that's correct? Just through the cross-examination, it was made clear to you that we were talking about a different scenario than, perhaps, the peacetime setting.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: No. You see, I do not view that in that way. We are talking about the crime of rape. The only thing is is that it happened in the territory of the former Yugoslavia while a conflict was ongoing. Myself or my colleagues never analysed rape as a war crime, as an act against international law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you have had no real experience with that, and when you came to this Tribunal, it was the first time that you had effectively been asked to make this type of discussion; in fact, it was cross-examination in Kunarac that brought this to your attention.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct to say that not only do I have no such experience, but no one else in the territory of the former state. Rape is a domestic crime and not an international crime, and therefore no one can have experience with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I was looking through your -- excuse me. Before I go on to that, there have been questions, though, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, of course, we're not looking at as former Yugoslav law, where detainees [sic] in district military courts have been found guilty of rape in 1992 actions involving the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska. Are you familiar with those cases? I think you were asked about them during cross in Kunarac. In principle, there has been some discussion but not necessarily under former Yugoslav law.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: There was rape in the former Yugoslavia and today, and that is evident from my report. But not once was it established that rape was committed for ethnic or some other such reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had mentioned cases where detainees in collection centres or in some other form of detention had possibly initiated sexual relations with guards. Has it been the position of your courts --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- thank you. Has it been the position of the courts in the former Yugoslavia that it is appropriate for policemen who have a relationship of, as it were, keeper to the detainees to have sexual relations with the detainees or prisoners? What has been the experience in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no such cases in the former Yugoslavia. You didn't understand me correctly. The cases that I have referred to were not processed, but people have spoken to me about it from their experience in life, not from court proceedings. Rape of persons in detention and persons held in custody were never found in the former Yugoslavia or the present-day Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Professor Bejatovic, the paper which you submitted on behalf of accused Radic was submitted January 30th, 2001. Now, that was after you testified in Kunarac. I went through the list of aggravating or possible aggravating factors and I did not notice the factors that you were asked about in Kunarac, such as detention status or -- I'm sorry, ethnically-motivated crime. Am I correct that those were not listed in this report filed in January even though they were discussed before the Tribunal, another Chamber of the Tribunal, in September? Those are not listed in your particular report before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: I compiled my report on the basis of an analysis of the judicial practice of the former Yugoslavia and the present-day Yugoslavia, and as I have already said, no such circumstances existed. Secondly, in writing this report, I did bear in mind the discussions in the Foca case. But in my report, I did not intentionally want to take it into consideration for two reasons: First, to discuss something in detail, one must have at one's disposal all the relevant evidence from the case, which I don't have; secondly, as far as I know, there is an assumption of innocence until a sentence becomes effective. Therefore, we cannot talk about that particular case as having been definitively judged, and that is why I did not analyse it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So the list on page 5 in the English of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Have I got two minutes or am I out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have, I think, already used at least three minutes over your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also deducted the time that the professor took to make corrections in his report. I keep insisting. Do you have a watch or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Surely there's someone in your team who can help you manage your time, Ms. Susan Somers. So your last question now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm sorry. My watch is perhaps not in sync with the rest of the Chamber's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Professor, this is the last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, I won't let that pass. There's a clock here and all we have to do is look at it. I don't control the time on the basis of my watch. There's this clock; it is the same clock that we are all looking at. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do apologise. I am five minutes behind. I apologise for that on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, the very last question is: The list of factors, then, that you did include on the English page 5 of your report - I won't list them out; they're there for everyone to see - you chose not to add the factors which you specifically were asked about in Kunarac, such as the detainee status and the other issue of ethnically motivated. That was a deliberate choice? That's my last question.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: My assignment in writing this report was to contribute to the practical implementation of Article 24 of this Statute. In accordance with the provisions of that article, all I can write in my report and testify about is based on the positive laws of the former Yugoslavia and present-day Yugoslavia and on the basis of judicial practice. We know what judicial practice is. So the Foca case cannot be taken into consideration because it is a case that has still not been terminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Susan Somers. Mr. Fila, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please describe the crime of rape according to the domestic law of the former SFRY and all the five republics; what the perpetrator needs to do, what applies to the victim? In just a few sentences, please.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: In response to the question of the Defence, I wish to state the following: The crime of rape, in present-day Yugoslavia, has been addressed in an identical manner as it was prescribed in the former Yugoslavia. Despite the fact that each of the republics that used to constitute the former Yugoslavia have regulated the crime of rape with their own laws, they are identical. The only difference was the passive subject in the Criminal Code of Slovenia. So it would be correct to say that this crime, in its basic form, in former and present Yugoslavia, is regulated in such a way: A crime exists if a male person, by use of force or threat, compels a female to submit to sexual intercourse by force and inflicts serious bodily injury upon her. Therefore, according to the former and present law, the active subject must use force or threat towards the passive subject or a threat against a close relative of that passive subject, and that force must be such as to create the impression of the victim that the crime will be committed. Also, that passive subject must resist as far as possible, showing that she does not comply even tacitly, that the person does not accept such treatment. So let me underline that this is the definition that applies in the laws of the former Yugoslavia and all the newly-created states.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it similarly dealt with in all other domestic legislations?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. The only difference is with respect to this passive subject, because some Criminal Codes envisaged that a passive subject may even be a wife. This is only exceptional. The other difference is the maximum penalty. As for all the other characteristics, they are almost identical in civilised societies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Professor Bejatovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to have the benefit of your experience and knowledge to enlighten me on a further question. You mentioned that rape against a vulnerable person or a physically weak person could be an aggravating circumstance, and you mentioned that judgements do not -- would not accept that if the victim contributed to the commission of the crime. Now, what would you call a contribution of the victim to the crime? I have in mind a case of a person where there is a great discrepancy of force, whether in prison or elsewhere, where the victim complies because the situation of the discrepancy does not leave any space for something else. Would you consider that as contribution?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that can be interpreted in that way. But on the other hand, we must bear in mind - and this is what we see from practice, not only in Yugoslavia, but in practice throughout the world - that a passive subject is -- an individual, if they are weak and appear weak, can give cause for the perpetration of that criminal act. So in a situation of that kind, we must look at the behaviour of that passive individual and look at all the circumstances. And I want to go back to the case that I mentioned a moment ago to the Prosecutor, when I talked -- discussed this situation in the former Yugoslavia with respect to these cases. It is normal for me to know that, for example, if in a collection centre - and there were collection centres of this kind, many of them - if there are people who are 20 years old, 30 years old, and spend one month there or two months there, and in many of the collection centres the conditions weren't so bad, it is normal that young individuals of this kind, after a month or two, have the desire for sexual intercourse. So we must look at that situation within that context as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. Now, you mentioned that there should always be, if I understood rightly, use of force or threat. Now, does it need to be a positive, active use or an implicit threat? There is a threat if you are in a superior position and the victim knows what could happen to her without even proceeding? What do you think? Should it be a real, actual threat or an implied threat, potential threat?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: The threat must be actual, real, and it must be continuous in time. So that threat, according to our Criminal Code, must last until the crime is carried out, until we consider that a crime has been committed. And I have described what we mean by the crime being committed. Now, if this threat stops before the crime has actually been committed, and after the threat the individual does not give resistance, as provided by law, to the perpetrator, then a crime does not exist. So the threat must be real, actual, and continuous until the crime has been considered to have been committed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Even if --

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: -- completion of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Even if the victim is vulnerable, as you said, or in a total situation of inferiority and weakness?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: I said what I meant by "weak" and "vulnerable" and the circumstances. These are all factors that must be assessed for each individual case and gone into individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: May I add just one more point, please. In Yugoslavia there is the practice - and I think it is a good practice, and it exists not only in Yugoslavia but elsewhere - two or three times we take students to visit the detention centres, prisons, and very often the students - and these are people we're talking about, 21, 22, young people - when they visit institutions where the women are the inmates, there are various indices, and this would provide an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In order to help me to understand better how the Yugoslavia law interprets force or threat of force, which you have said is a prerequisite or a material requirement for rape, consider the following situation: If somebody is in prison, detention, or under the at least physical authority of someone else, say a guard, and the guard comes to the prisoner and says, "I have the power to get you out of here more quickly than you will otherwise if you submit to me," but there is no -- there's no threat of beating or that sort of thing, but, "If you want to get out of here, if you want to see your family again, then submit to me," would that be considered rape under Yugoslavian law?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: In a case of that kind, there is no rape as a crime, according to Yugoslav law, because for the crime of rape to exist, the resistance on the part of the passive subject, the woman victim, must be actual, serious, and continuous, as I said before. In your case, there is no such resistance and therefore no crime of rape, according to our law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You have answered my question, but I would add: I do not think that is by any means universal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Professor, when you say that the resistance must be continuous - what is the term? - a quo and ad quem?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: The passive victim -- the criminal act does not consider to have been completed -- the passive victim must not agree to it. And according to criminal law, and not only Yugoslav criminal law, a crime has been committed only when there is penetration of the male sex organ into the female sex organ. Up until that point, that alleged victim or passive subject must resist, must put up resistance to the best of their physical abilities. If, once the act has been committed, she ceases to give resistance or does not give resistance, then there is no crime of rape; the crime of rape is not recognised in those cases. And that is one of the reasons why in our judicial practice, as in the judicial practice of the former Yugoslavia, you have a relatively large difference between the accused -- people accused of rape and people actually found guilty and sentenced for rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I understood you properly, Professor. The continuousness that you say must exist, the continuousness in the victim's resistance that you talked about, where does it start and where does it end? Where does the resistance start and where does the resistance end for us to be able to consider that violation and rape has taken place?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Resistance must take place at the precise moment when any act has been taken by the active subject vis-à-vis the passive subject with the aim of performing this crime. So the moment that woman is a victim, when the passive subject has understood that she is going to be raped, she must start setting up resistance immediately in the manner I described, and that resistance -- she must keep up that resistance until the act has been committed. If this passive subject offered resistance but the resistance was not continuous, that is to say, it ceased at the last moment, when the two sexual organs were conjoined, then there is no crime of rape. And that is the united stand of Yugoslav criminal theory and judicial practice, not only in this present Yugoslavia but in the former Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spoke about physical resistance, Professor. Does the law of ex-Yugoslavia or the present Yugoslavia consider other types of resistance, not only physical resistance?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If the passive subject was not able to set up physical resistance, then there should be all other types of resistance which are in line with the capabilities of the passive subject and correspond to the passive subject's make-up. So it doesn't only mean physical resistance. Theoretically speaking, we can think of other forms of resistance. For example, a young man and a young woman going out in a car together. They drive in a car together and they come into a situation and the young woman cannot give physical resistance, but she can call help, she can call out, "Help," she can resort to other forms of resistance. But the resistance, as I say, must be adequate and suited to the circumstances. If the passive subject does not offer any kind of resistance within these limiting frameworks, then there is no crime of rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on to another aspect. Imagine, please, Professor, that somebody has read a piece of paper, a newspaper, which states that in order for rape to have been committed, the crime of rape to have been committed, the victim must offer physical resistance. In the meantime, he finds himself in a situation in which the victim does not offer physical resistance but says, "I don't want to. I don't wish to." In the meantime, the active subject has in his mind that there must be physical resistance and he consumes the act; he goes ahead with the act. Is that rape or is it not?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: We cannot consider the crime of rape to have taken place if the passive subject just says, "I don't want to," without resorting to anything else. For the crime of rape to exist, not only according to our own criminal legislation, the passive subject must set up adequate resistance. If the victim just says, "I don't want to," and doesn't take any other measures of resistance, then it is clear that there is no crime of rape, and that is normal. And nobody, I think, in Yugoslavia, and anybody else, would question a situation of that kind, would consider it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, can we conclude that from that point of view, if the passive subject, if the victim says, "I do not want to" but does not offer physical resistance, does that mean that she is in fact saying, "Yes, I want to"?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if she was able to offer resistance. If she was able to offer resistance and has just said, "I don't want to," then it's normal that in fact that would imply what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, Professor. What does Yugoslav legislation have to say on active and passive subject with respect to sex?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the crime of rape, the Yugoslav legislation provides for other forms of criminal acts, crimes, contrary to nature, crimes contrary to nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Professor. What I wanted to ask was this: Let us consider this hypothesis and its curiosity on my part. For example, where the victim or the passive subject is a witness, can we inverse the situation and have violation where the passive subject is a man? We have considered the matter where the passive subject is the woman. What about the other sex?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Criminal legislation does not provide for cases of that kind, although there have been theoretical discussions. But for the time being, the law does not provide for that, because we say that it is when -- the law provides for when a male, a man, does this act towards a female, and we considered it in wedlock. For the moment, the male cannot be the passive subject of rape, for the moment, as the law stands at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I think Madam Judge Wald has an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you for indulging me. I just have one question to help me understand, again a hypothetical. If a guard, in a situation of detention, says to the prisoner, "I want you to have sex with me, and if you resist, I'm going to beat you," and the prisoner goes ahead and submits, does not resist, thereby bringing down a beating, is that rape or is she under a duty to resist even at the cost of a promised beating?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: In a situation of that kind, she has the duty to resist for the crime to be rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Even if she's going to be beaten and has been told and has reason to believe from past experience that his threat of a beating can be brought down? Is that really Yugoslavian law?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what does she know that she will actually be beaten?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Because she may have seen other people in the same situation beaten in the past.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no cases of that kind, as far as I know. But in that particular case, she would have to offer some resistance, some sort of resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the norms of Yugoslav criminal law are clear there on that point. The situation would be quite different if that individual - and this is a hypothesis. Let's take the hypothesis - if she were tied, if she were bound, her arms, her legs, her mouth, then she would not be able to set up resistance of any kind. But in all other situation she can offer resistance, and she is duty-bound to offer resistance to prevent the crime from taking place, the act from taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What if he says, "If you don't submit to me, I'm going to kill you," and he's a guard; he's got a pistol in his belt. She has to take that chance of being killed?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Even in a case of that kind she must assess whether he would actually do it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: The fact itself, only that fact, cannot be taken into consideration for the crime to be rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to insist on one point in this matter. I don't know if I understood the answer properly. So even if there is the threat of death, of a killing, if somebody -- if the active subject threatens to kill the passive subject -- let us say a man is threatening a woman, he is threatening her with death, to kill her if she does not accept to have sexual relations with him, and if the woman really believes this, that she's going to die unless she consents, if she does not offer physical resistance, is that rape or is it not, Professor? Is that considered rape or not?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: I personally feel that this is a theoretical construction. Viewed from the aspects of theory, that could be so, but that is theory, the realm of theory. It is an assumption, a hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I apologise for interrupting you, Professor. This is not a theory. It does happen in real life. In many circumstances, a man says to a woman, "Unless you consent, I will kill you."

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but there are many other situations, and not only in our own legal practice, but others. A man says to a woman, "I'm going to kill you. I'm going to throw you out of the window," from the fifth or sixth floor, and she doesn't submit, so therefore -- and he doesn't do anything. So that -- you cannot prove intent there. So this passive subject must weigh the situation up, weigh the danger up, weigh the threat up, and, in keeping with that entire situation, to see whether he actually means it or not. Because practice tells us otherwise. There are many cases where a young girl goes to a young man's flat and says she doesn't consent, and he threatens to throw her out the window and nothing comes of that threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question. Let us look at this problem from the other side, from another angle. If I understood you correctly, you said, when giving the definition of rape, I think you said that for rape there must be force exerted, and you also said menace, threat. What I want to know is: Do you have to have force and threat or just one of those two, for the definition, in your Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: I did not speak about my own definition, I spoke about the legal definition. Therefore, according to our own laws, it is threat or force, not both. Threat or force. But both must be of the kind that I mentioned. So it is not cumulative, it is either/or, either one or the other. That is the legal formulation, it is not my own definition and formulation. It is the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I think we ought to wind up. But Judge Fouad Riad has an additional question. Otherwise, we would be discussing this forever. We are a Tribunal, we are not a faculty of law. That is why we'll have to put a time limit. Otherwise, we could go on discussing this question for a long time. I did myself ask the question you were answering as a professor, but if you were a judge, this would be a hypothesis. Judge Fouad Riad, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a point, because in your answers, you were concentrating on the intent of the person committing the act. Now, this intent, the victim cannot definitely, sufficiently know it. But would it be enough if the circumstances give a likelihood of the seriousness of the threat?

utterances.speaker: STANKO BEJATOVIC
utterances.text: Intent is one of the elements which, according to our Criminal Code, is taken into account when sentencing is weighed up. But that intent is analysed with respect to all the circumstances related to a case. So perhaps the victim cannot gauge the intent itself at the point in time. If a man has raped just one woman, then that is one intent; if he has raped more than one woman, then the intent is quite different. So intent or motive must be ascertained on the basis of an analysis of the case in its entirety, with all its factors and circumstances. What is important for our Criminal Code is that no circumstance that I spoke about in my report, and no circumstance from the Criminal Code viewed from the aspects of the Criminal Code, is provided for in advance as aggravating or mitigating. The character that this factor takes on in each individual case is a matter of that concrete case and circumstance. But what is meritorious for the Court is to see how they are behind, to analyse the case as a whole with all the factors and circumstances - not only those stipulated in Article 41 of the Criminal Code but all the other circumstances which were characteristic for that particular case - and on the basis of this all-embracing, comprehensive analysis will a judgement and sentencing take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Fila on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let us just differentiate between something. To your question, whether the victim must be a woman, the answer was something else. There is a crime when a man rapes another man but it is not called rape. There is another term used for that case, when it is a man violating a man, if that is at all of assistance to you. Perhaps because of the translation, the interpretation, it is this serious threat. If the professor allows me, I can answer. If serious threat existed that there would be bodily harm, then, of course, the crime of rape is recognised. But it is up to the Court to assess whether the threat is serious or not serious. That is up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila, we shall have to finish because otherwise we will enter into a discussion about threat, whether it is serious, semi-serious, or whatever. Thank you, Mr. Fila, for your assistance on that point. Mr. Professor Bejatovic, we have no further questions to ask you. We are satisfied with the clarifications you made, explanations you gave. We thank you for coming here and wish you a lot of good deliberation and actions when you go back to your country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. But may I be allowed to add something to what Mr. Fila said? And you interrupted me. The Yugoslav Criminal Code, in addition to the crime of rape where the passive subject can only be a woman, there is another criminal act -- two other criminal acts where the passive subject may be a man. But that is a subject apart, it is a separate area. If you need to, we can speak about that. So the sexual freedom of the man from this aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Professor, we are satisfied with what we have heard so far. Thank you for coming, and the usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I think it is time for a lunch break. That is what you were going to suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We accept your suggestion, and we'll adjourn for 50 minutes. Please take a look at the clock in the courtroom, and the 50 minutes is based on that clock. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Right. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence calls its last witness, the psychiatrist, Dr. van den Bussche, and Ms. Somers will be able to use my 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but not abuse them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that you can hear me now. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration which the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Doctor. Very well. Dr. van den Bussche, you are here to provide some clarifications relative to your psychiatric finding. Mr. Fila, who is the Defence counsel, has submitted your report as your testimony, and we shall now proceed to your cross-examination, which will be conducted by Ms. Somers. Thank you very much for coming and accepting to answer these questions. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... English, that is fine with you?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell us, please: When you received the assignment to do a joint report, was it your understanding that you would interview the subject Radic jointly or simply come to joint -- to conclusions in consultation one with the other?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we didn't know each other, and we had a very limited time to perform the assessment. So after the initial phone call from me to Belgrade, I heard that Ms. Najman was coming to -- my colleague, Ms. Najman, was coming to Holland about within a week. But then at the last minute I got another call that she was delayed, so we had only six days left to perform the assessment together. And we made the first appointment to meet each other in front of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Doctor, to interrupt you. My question was: Was it your understanding that your joint report would be a report involving a simultaneous joint interview of the subject --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Joint written, joint written, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But not simultaneous interview of the subject? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: The written question is joint written report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And separate, independent interviews with the accused; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, that did not happen, did it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Well, in a certain way it happened. She -- Ms. Najman saw Mr. Radic the day before and she asked questions - I don't know which one - and she was together with me when we talked again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But at no time did you, one-on-one with Radic, have your interview; Dr. Najman was always present. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. She did -- she talked with Mr. Radic alone and she talked together with me, but she didn't ask any questions. I asked the questions and she was listening. And because I asked the questions in Dutch, so the translator interpreted the questions in Yugoslavian and she was following -- listening to what I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But she was always --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: She wasn't intervening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: She was always with you in a room when you talked with Radic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You never had a one-on-one, independent interview without --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: She --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Could you make pauses, please, between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Radic. You had never met alone with Radic; is that correct? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: I haven't been alone with Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You indicated on one of the pages of your report that you had had contact -- on page -- it looks like - let me see - 4 of the report, you indicated that, at the top of it, in English: "Since this was a medical, psychiatric assessment, I, Bernard van den Bussche, consulted the medical service of the prison by telephone in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. order to verify the medical problems experienced by the defendant." You were aware, then, that you could have contact to communicate with the medical service of the detention facility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you also indicated in your report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness please make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the position, but that you were aware there was a nurse there and at some point you spoke with a nurse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: No. I tried to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please slow down, Ms. Somers, please, because there are interpreters here working, even though you speak the same language. So the interpreters need you to make a pause between the question and an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. van den Bussche. You did not consult directly with the medical doctor, Valke?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: I tried to contact the medical doctor, but he wasn't there, and I had to finish my report in two days, so the only possibility was to talk with the nurse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On page 12 of your report you have made a comment that says: "His mood was slightly agitated and indignant, but with an evident somber undertone. His emotions were close to the surface. When we started to talk about his wife and children, he began to cry. To a certain extent there were and are suicidal thoughts." I turn your attention to page 6 of the report, where Radic says to you: "My wife has been here twice. Once the Red Cross paid for her to come, my son too, and once a cousin. What can I say? How are they going to survive? It is only thanks to Ms. Vera Petrovic, a psychiatrist with whom I have regularly spoken, that I am still alive. Otherwise I would have hanged myself. I've thought of it several times. What's holding me back?" Now, Dr. Najman, your colleague, also submitted a report in which she, on page 6 of hers - and I hope you have read it - indicated likewise there are discrete test signs that could indicate the danger of suicide. Two people have made this observation. Did you report these findings to the medical service? Is there a report that you submitted to the medical service about ideas concerning suicide which you describe in the present tense, on page 12 of your report: "To an extent there were and are"?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't phone or contact the medical doctor because, in my opinion, there are suicidal thoughts but not in a very severe way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It appears from your report that you have taken at face value almost everything that Mr. Radic may have told you. Is there a particular reason that you did not take at face value this talking about suicide? How did you distinguish what's to be accepted and what is not?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: I have taken nothing at face value, because that's also not possible, because I don't have collateral data. I almost have not any collateral data besides the general indictment. So that means that when I have to give -- to tell you what Mr. Radic is saying, those are his words, and I'm not in the possibility to check those words, because I can't talk with family, I don't see witness accounts; I only have the general indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you mention to Dr. Najman your concerns or your observations about the suicide? Did you speak about those?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: We talked about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did she tell you about --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: But can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No. Did she tell you about a patient whom she also worked with in this Tribunal named Slavko Dokmanovic? Did she mention Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did she tell you that he, in fact, committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And after having learned that, you took no action whatsoever to notify the officials, the Chamber, the registry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: That's not completely correct. I told you before it was my opinion -- there is a difference between somebody who is very suicidal or not, and it's my profession to check if somebody is very severe suicidal or not. And besides that, I had signs that Mr. Radic had a good relation in the United Nations Detention Unit with the psychiatrist, and he told me about that. So if I would have the impression that he would be very severe depressed -- and I said in my report that he has not a severe depression. He has dysthymia. That means there's a mild depression. So if I would say he has dysthymia and he is very suicidal, I would say something very wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, that psychiatrist is Dr. Petrovic, about whom Mr. Radic spoke to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware from Dr. Najman that that was the psychiatrist who testified about the condition of Slavko Dokmanovic before he committed suicide?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, please, you indicated that you didn't have -- you never had access to many materials. I think you just called them collateral materials. You had an indictment?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: I had only the general indictment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that at the time you interviewed Mr. Radic, that the trial had been going on for some two months and that there was witness testimony?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes, but I find all the witness testimony -- I received more information from the Registry -- I received more information from the Internet than from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You're suggesting that there's no value to the testimony of people who claim to have been the object of various acts?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Within -- we had only six days to perform the report. That means that we received the general indictment, that we have to talk with the accused, and that we have to write a joint written report. That means that the value of our report is limited. You are asking me questions about the limitations of our report. So I can't do more than I have done within the limited time this Court has given me to perform the report. And there are many restrictions to my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Six days are how many working hours, please? A number.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: How many? I worked about 60 hours -- I worked about 60 hours in six days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: But it's not enough time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that, according to professional standards, 60 hours is not sufficient time to conclude what you had to do in concert with another mental health professional? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, did you ask to see the videotape of the record of interview given by Mr. Radic to an investigator of this Tribunal not too long after his arrest? Did you ask to see that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: I didn't know that there was a videotape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have testified in other cases in this Tribunal - Jelisic, for example - haven't you?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You know the procedures of this Tribunal, do you not?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: In a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you make any effort to try to get ahold of the direct examination of Mr. Radic that he gave at the very beginning of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: I tried to get as much possible information and I asked the Registry to give me all kinds of relevant information. So I am -- that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So your sole source of information was Mladjo Radic himself and, apparently, the indictment; would that be it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, the conclusions --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I'm speaking very rapidly because of time constraints. I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The conclusion which you came to at the end of your report, on page 12, was that conclusion a diagnosis contained in the tool which you indicated you used called the DSM-4, which is Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fourth edition?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you're indicating that the conclusion which you came to, which was Mr. Radic was a man -- let's see. How is it phrased? "The wrong man in the wrong place at the wrong time." Is that found in the DSM-4?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: No. I tell you, first of all, there is an error in the translation of the -- of my Dutch version to the English one, because in my Dutch version, I wrote in English "an ordinary man at the wrong place at the wrong time," and not "the wrong man." That's first of all. So that's an error. I wrote "an ordinary man," and that's crucial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that in the DSM-4?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: That's not in the DSM-4. And the DSM-4, I write about dysthymia. Because an ordinary man is not a person who has a disorder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You call it dysthymia. Is it dysthymic disorder you're referring to? Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a mild form of depression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Najman used not the DSM-4, she used a system, I think it's called --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: The ICD-10.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, the ICD-10, which is from the World Health Organisation, a very different analytical tool, diagnostic tool; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Not a very different diagnostic tool. In all our handbooks, there is -- the DSM-4 and the ICD-10 are mixed, so there is about 80 per cent overlap, 20 per cent not. But in regard to dysthymia or dysthymic disorders or personality disorders, they are the same, both in the national diagnostic systems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you used separate diagnostic tools and came to a conclusion that you got only through the information given to you by Mladjo Radic, within the presence of Ana Najman, who is culturally and linguistically familiar with Radic? Is that how it is, as you use the term, in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: No. We used the same diagnostic instruments. There was no difference between the diagnosis she made and I made.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On page 13 of your report, essentially what you do is indicate to the Chamber, because this is for whom this report is intended, "I do not have the exact answer" - and the question, of course, was how ordinary men can become ruthless war criminals - "I do not have the exact answer. All I can do is recommend reading on this matter with which you are probably familiar." And you proceed on page 13 to give a reading list. Is this a profession -- is a typical, for you, professionally rendered opinion or diagnosis, responsive to what the Registry asked you to produce? Is this how you always do it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: No, no. I just gave -- this is not a typical reading list. These are just a few of the books of a typical reading list. But I mentioned them only -- I mentioned only these five books because they focus a little bit on the subject of "ordinary man," but they don't focus on the overall problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, did you do your own testing, or did you rely on the testing of Ana Najman?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: I did my own testing. But we are not two of one kind, we are two of a different kind. So that means that my instrument is the clinical interview and her instrument is far more the psychological testing. What you do afterwards is to resemble your clinical, professional interview, or my clinical, professional interview, you discuss it, compare it with her testing. So we tried to do our job independent of each other, and then after discussing, you try to write a joint written report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that what you did was a structured, clinical interview in accordance with professional standards?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes, because that's my profession since about 15 years. And I'm the quality manager of the forensic assessments in Holland. I've performed about 1.000 forensic assessments. We also discussed this matter last year at the World Psychiatric Association Congress in Madrid, and I discussed it with my colleagues of the American Association for Psychiatry and Law, and they all had some ethical questions about the limited time and possibilities we were given by this Court to perform our job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Additional questions, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard this quick cross-examination, and what I should like to know, in the end, is whether Dr. van den Bussche accepts this report as a joint report drawn by him and Mrs. Najman, and whether he still stands by all that the report says.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Judge Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. van den Bussche, good afternoon. I just understood at the end of your testimony that -- you mentioned the American Association for Psychiatry and Law, they all had some ethical questions about the limited time and possibilities you were given by this Court to perform your job. What were these ethical questions?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Well, all my colleagues were a little bit amazed by the fact that we had to do the job within the limited period of six days, because in a regular -- in a regular court case in one of the countries like Europe -- in Europe or in the States, a forensic expert is given at least a few weeks to perform a job. You try to receive -- you are given as much data by the court, and it's not in a way that you have to ask to receive data, no; they are provided and there is an unlimited access to data. In the case of the assessment of Radic, the forensic assessment of Radic, I was limited in my experience. It's also very important that we are -- that you have the opportunity to talk several times with the defendant in a few weeks, because there is, of course, a difference when you talk only once with somebody and if you have the possibility to talk twice or three times. Because in the first -- the first time you talk to somebody, it's not wise to confront somebody. It's better to wait with that, for example, as a technique until the last time you speak to somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: And also -- also another ethical question is what I've seen in this Court, with all due respect for you, is that sometimes only one psychiatric examination is asked; another time, there is a psychiatric and psychological examination asked; sometimes, there is psychiatric examination asked -- assessment asked, performed by two psychiatrists. That's something we, as psychiatrists, internationally, don't understand so much, because you have to regulate that. In our international standards, it's usually that in a severe case there is always a psychiatric and psychological report together, and not only a psychiatric report; and that, for example, even in very severe court cases, there is an examination of the social circumstances by a social worker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, still the fact remains that you made a report, and you stand by this report.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: I stand by this report in the limit -- in the limitations of the time I was provided, because we -- in terms of diagnosis, I had enough time. But that's -- but with regard to the other questions, it's far more difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: For instance, when you spoke of -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes. If you asked me what is the present mental state of the defendant, then it is like a snapshot, and for a snapshot, you need not that much time. But if you ask, for example, what are the possibilities for resocialisation, then I need far more data, material, to answer that. That's more like a movie. Or if you ask somebody responsible for the crimes, that's -- therefore, to answer a question like that, you also need far more data. So in regards to the diagnosis of my report of Radic, I had enough time. But in regard to other questions, I think my report is restricted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you had very positive conclusions. You said, "The suicidal thoughts are not severe."

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes, because that's my profession, to check that. If his depression -- if he really had depression, then it would be another matter. But he had a mild dysthymia, and that is something that -- he had dysthymia or a dysthymic disorder, so that's not severe depression. It's a slightly, slightly depressed mood. He also had an -- and also I checked, of course, his suicidal thoughts, because if somebody is suicidal, then you also ask, "If you would try to commit suicide, how would you do it?" Mr. Radic had no plans, he had no crystalised plans to commit suicide. It was more an attempt for help, a cry. But from my experience, he was not somebody -- he's not somebody who is going to commit suicide on the short term. It may be different when he's -- when he would receive a long sentence. And then you have to see how he's going to be during his detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you had enough time to reach such a finding.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, we had enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What about when you said that he is an ordinary man in the wrong place at the wrong time? What made you reach that fact?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: What I mean by "ordinary man" is that he is somebody -- he's a primitive man without a personality disorder, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What about the wrong place and the wrong time?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: The war circumstances. So an ordinary man or a man without a personality disorder or a man without a severe psychiatric disorder in very stressful war circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean that could happen to any man, any normal person?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Dr. van den Bussche, I have two questions. One: Did you agree with everything that Ms. Najman had in her separate report? Let me give you a few examples, although I don't have it in front of me, and I hope my memory is correct, but yours may be more accurate. But I believe that she referred to Mr. Radic as a person who had great respect for authority and was not likely to flaunt authority or to go against authority or to initiate a kind of proactive conduct that would be against rules or authority. But my basic question to you is: Did you agree with all of her conclusions, or was it more of a, well, those are the conclusions she draws from her material, these are the conclusions I draw from my material, and there isn't anything contradictory in them? If you would just explain a little bit what the nature of the agreement between you about each other's reports was.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: The nature of the agreement is, first of all, that we both came to the same conclusion in regard to his mood disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: That there was a mild form of depression called dysthymia, or dysthymic disorder, so there was no disagreement. And then in regard to his personality traits, we had, in fact, the same opinion and we used maybe different words. Sometimes we both had the opinion that Mr. Radic was a primitive man --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you say "primitive," maybe you could tell me a little more what you mean.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Primitive is not mature, yes? Primitive, simple, not mature. That's in fact another word, yes? Or you can say a little bit childish in a certain way. Further on, we agreed in regard to the other traits, like that he is, in our opinion, obedient to authority and that he is passive-dependent. That means he is not such an independent man. And further on, we found separately no signs of specially anti-social disorder personality traits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My second question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My second question is: You've given us a little bit of an indication, but I'd like you, if possible, to elaborate, if you wish to. If you would have had more time, if you had had what you consider to be the appropriate amount of time that you would normally expect in an evaluation of this kind -- you've mentioned that you would have had other interviews, you would have had a series of interviews to get more of an evolving picture, and you've also mentioned that you might have tried to get more information about -- of a social background kind of thing. Are there -- what other elements of a more detailed evaluation that you didn't have time for here, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: The evaluation of the witness accounts, for example. I have only the personal information of Mr. Radic and I've seen the general indictment, but I don't have seen [sic] the witness accounts. And in this case, in a certain way it was for me easy, because Mr. Radic was denying the facts. But if he would have said, "I have committed the crimes," then I would have been in a difficult position, because then I have to only make a conclusion on his comments about the crimes and I have no information about witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one follow-up question on that and then I'll be through, because it's come up in the cross-examination, both of you and of Ms. Najman. But I'm wondering, from your expert point of view, if you just read witness transcripts, which would -- or you watched -- maybe you could watch a video - I don't know - of witnesses, don't you have an expert problem too in evaluating whether they're telling the truth or credible or -- when you haven't seen them and talked to them?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course, but I don't look at those interviews as a judge. You know, in fact, I'm not -- it's not my job to say if it's true or not true. So I look at other aspects of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD VAN DEN BUSSCHE
utterances.text: In the Dutch system we are used to that, so we see all the interviews of the investigating judge or the police.
